title: Permutation-Equivariant Flow Matching for Alignment-Free Neural Weight Generation

paper.title: Permutation-Equivariant Flow Matching for Alignment-Free Neural Weight Generation
paper.abstract:
Abstract A
trained
neural network can be represented by a parameter vector in
high dimensions.
Learning distributions over these vectors enables the
generation of new models across various tasks and architectures. A central challenge is permutation symmetry: permuting hidden neurons
can produce distant parameter vectors representing the same function.
This introduces variations that a generative model must
account for when learning from trained networks. Existing methods typically address this
using networks derived from a common base model or
costly approximate neuron alignment.
We instead parameterize a flow-matching velocity field with a permutation-equivariant Graph Meta Network, enabling direct learning from independently trained networks without alignment. Extensive experiments show that our method closely reproduces the joint statistics of accuracy, functional similarity, and weight similarity of independently trained collections, providing evidence of generation beyond checkpoint memorization. A single conditional model also generates task-specific networks
on
heterogeneous architectures and generalizes to unseen hidden-width configurations.
On a tabular domain-shift task, intermediate conditioning produces individual networks with performance comparable to logit ensembles across both domains. Taken together, our results show how permutation equivariance enables
learning
from diverse collections of independently trained networks without permutation alignment.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Trained network weights have emerged as a new data modality ( Unterthiner et al., 2020 ; Eilertsen et al., 2020 ; Schürholt et al., 2021 ; Navon et al., 2023 ; Navon et al., 2024 ; Lim et al., 2024 ; Putterman et al., 2024 ; Gelberg et al., 2025 ; Dayan et al., 2026 ; Knyazev et al., 2025 ; Tran et al., 2025 ; Kofinas et al., 2024 ; Kalogeropoulos et al., 2024 ) . Weight-space generative modeling promises a paradigm shift: rather than optimize neural networks, we could sample them directly from a learned distribution. Weight generation, rather than optimization, may unlock powerful capabilities, most notably conditional generation, allowing us to synthesize networks tailored to specific datasets, architectures, or domains ( Wang et al., 2026 ; Han et al., 2026 ) . Despite this potential, learning the distribution of independently trained neural networks remains a challenge. Figure 1: Hidden-unit permutations preserve the network function. Colors track each hidden unit and its incident weights. Ideally, we wish to train a generative model on large-scale network collections, spanning diverse tasks and architectures, to capture the distribution of diverse solutions. However, two functionally identical networks can have different weight matrices due to arbitrary hidden-neuron ordering (Figure 1 ). This is a practical concern as repositories like Hugging Face ( Wolf et al., 2020 ) host diverse trained networks without a common ordering or shared initialization. As such, weight-space symmetries, transformations that change weights yet preserve the function, especially permutation symmetries, are ubiquitous and thus form a fundamental obstacle in weight-space generation. To avoid this issue, prior works alter the network collections used for training. Post-hoc approaches approximately align compatible training networks to a common reference ( Ainsworth et al., 2022 ) . A priori methods instead create artificially the training collection so that alignment is not needed, typically by sampling checkpoints along the optimization trajectory of a single network ( Wang et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2025 ; Erkoç et al., 2023 ) . These strategies require either compatible architectures for alignment or control over how the training collection is constructed, restricting their applicability to existing repositories of independently trained networks. Many generators impose further limitations through fixed-dimensional parameterizations, restricting their direct reuse across architectures ( Wang et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2025 ; Erkoç et al., 2023 ; Schürholt et al., 2022 ; Schürholt et al., 2024 ; Gupta et al., 2026 ) . Moreover, sample efficiency and memorization remain challenges even within these restricted settings ( Zeng et al., 2026 ; Navon et al., 2023 ; Navon et al., 2024 ; Shamsian et al., 2024 ) . Figure 2: Method overview. A shared velocity field v 𝜽 ​ ( 𝒢 , 𝒘 t , t , c ) v_{{\bm{\theta}}}({\mathcal{G}},{\bm{w}}_{t},t,c) , trained on unaligned networks, generates weights conditioned on architecture 𝒢 {\mathcal{G}} and task c c . States 𝒘 t {\bm{w}}_{t} and 𝒚 t {\bm{y}}_{t} belong to different architectures. A hidden-unit permutation 𝑷 g {\bm{P}}_{g} permutes the trajectory and its velocities, producing functionally equivalent networks (upper pair). We advocate a switch to equivariant tools, which are natural for symmetries. Following recent advances in graph metanetworks ( Lim et al., 2024 ; Knyazev et al., 2025 ; Kofinas et al., 2024 ; Kalogeropoulos et al., 2024 ) , we represent neural networks as graphs, adopt Flow Matching (FM) ( Lipman et al., 2023 ) , and parameterize the velocity field with a Graph Meta Network (GMN) designed to be equivariant with weight-space permutations (Figure 2 ). We motivate this inductive bias by showing that permutation-invariant initialization and equivariant training yield a permutation-equivariant optimal FM velocity field. On up to 100 ​ K 100\mathrm{K} independently trained networks, our model generates networks with joint accuracy and similarity statistics much closer to the training network distribution than existing works. We further show that our method can interpolate across domain shifts, process heterogeneous architectures, and generate weights at unseen hidden widths. Our main contributions can be summarized as follows: 1. Alignment-free generation beyond memorization. We parameterize a flow-matching velocity field with a permutation-equivariant GMN to learn directly from independently trained networks without alignment. Our proposed joint quality measure shows that generated networks closely match independently trained networks in performance and similarity, providing evidence against checkpoint memorization. 2. Heterogeneous architecture generation. A single flow generates weights across heterogeneous architectures and generalizes to unseen widths, without retraining or architecture-specific changes to the generator. 3. Conditional weight-space traversal. We demonstrate conditional generation across diverse tasks and domain shifts, showing that our flow generalizes to unseen conditions and synthesizes single unified models on par with logit ensembling.

sections.heading: 3 Related Efforts
sections.text: Early work showed that neural networks can learn to generate other neural networks by producing their weights ( Ha et al., 2016 ; Bertinetto et al., 2016 ; Jia et al., 2016 ) . Building on this, many efforts were made toward modeling the distributions of the weights themselves. Weight-Space Generative Models. Hyper-Representations and SANE use autoencoders to learn latent representations for weight generation ( Schürholt et al., 2022 ; Schürholt et al., 2024 ) . P-diff ( Wang et al., 2024 ) combines an autoencoder with latent diffusion, a framework extended with dataset conditioning in D2NWG ( Soro et al., 2025 ) . DeepWeightFlow (DWF) operates directly in weight space, with optional PCA compression ( Gupta et al., 2026 ) , while RPG scales generation through parameter tokenization and recurrent diffusion ( Wang et al., 2025 ) . Post-Hoc Alignment. Post-hoc approaches align existing checkpoints before training the generator. SANE ( Schürholt et al., 2024 ) and DWF ( Gupta et al., 2026 ) use canonicalization methods such as Git Re-Basin ( Ainsworth et al., 2022 ) , which approximately matches weights to a common reference. Erdogan (2025) explores permutation-equivariant FM on MLP trajectory checkpoints, incorporating Git Re-Basin into the training pipeline. For Git Re-Basin, matching assumes equivalent architectures, limiting its direct applicability to heterogeneous collections. A Priori Alignment. A priori methods artificially reduce permutation variability by building dependent networks. P-diff ( Wang et al., 2024 ) collects checkpoints along an optimization trajectory, a recipe also adopted in D2NWG ( Soro et al., 2025 ) . RPG ( Wang et al., 2025 ) similarly collects fine-tuning checkpoints from pretrained models. NNiT ( Kim et al., 2026 ) builds its structurally aligned training collection using a Graph HyperNetwork with a convolutional decoder. Such recipes assume control on creating dependent networks, limiting their applicability to existing repositories of independently trained checkpoints. Weight-Space Memorization. Zeng et al. (2026) found substantial memorization in P-diff ( Wang et al., 2024 ) , Hyper-Representations ( Schürholt et al., 2022 ) , HyperDiffusion ( Erkoç et al., 2023 ) , and G.pt ( Peebles et al., 2022 ) . In the settings studied, they found that these methods largely reproduced training checkpoints or their interpolations and did not outperform simple weight perturbation or averaging baselines in jointly achieving high performance and novelty.

sections.text: Our goal is to learn weight distributions from independently trained networks without assuming a common hidden-unit ordering. We motivate our generator through the symmetry of these distributions, then construct a shared equivariant velocity field across architectures and tasks. Notation. sections.heading: 4.3 Evaluating Generation Beyond Memorization
sections.text: Figure 4: Generation joint evaluation (conceptual). Memorized networks perform well; nonfunctional networks have low similarity. We seek agreement with training networks in both metrics. To assess generation beyond checkpoint memorization ( Zeng et al., 2026 ) , we compare joint task-performance, functional-similarity, and weight-similarity statistics of generated and independently trained networks. High performance can reflect copying, while low similarity can reflect nonfunctional outputs (Figure 4 ). For a fixed task and architecture, 𝒯 = { 𝒘 i } i = 1 N \mathcal{T}=\{{\bm{w}}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N} is the training collection. Task performance and functional similarity. We use test accuracy, or positive-class ROC AUC, as the task-performance score S task ​ ( 𝒘 ) S_{\mathrm{task}}({\bm{w}}) , and maximum error-IoU as functional similarity S func ​ ( 𝒘 , 𝒯 ) S_{\mathrm{func}}({\bm{w}};\mathcal{T}) , which is a reference measure of error-pattern similarity in weight-space generation ( Zeng et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2024 ; Gupta et al., 2026 ) . See Appendix B for a definition. Weight similarity. Functional similarity may be fooled by small training weight perturbations. We thus also measure matched Weight Cosine Similarity (WCS). Let 𝑷 i {\bm{P}}_{i} be the hidden-unit permutation found by aligning 𝒘 i {\bm{w}}_{i} to 𝒘 {\bm{w}} using Git Re-Basin (weight variant). We define WCS ⁡ ( 𝒘 , 𝒯 ) = max 𝒘 i ∈ 𝒯 ⁡ 𝒘 ⊤ ​ 𝑷 i ​ 𝒘 i ‖ 𝒘 ‖ 2 ​ ‖ 𝑷 i ​ 𝒘 i ‖ 2 . \mathrm{WCS}({\bm{w}};\mathcal{T})=\max_{{\bm{w}}_{i}\in\mathcal{T}}\frac{{\bm{w}}^{\top}{\bm{P}}_{i}{\bm{w}}_{i}}{\|{\bm{w}}\|_{2}\|{\bm{P}}_{i}{\bm{w}}_{i}\|_{2}}. (12) Joint Wasserstein Similarity. Separate average scores mask how performance and similarity vary together. Instead, we combine for each network the three scores: task performance and functional and weight similarities. We create an (inter) unalignable collection of 100 ​ K 100\mathrm{K} independently trained MLPs on 20 20 tabular datasets from OpenML ( Bischl et al., 2021 ) , with 5 ​ K 5\mathrm{K} networks per dataset. The collection spans 16 16 architectures, varying in input dimensionality, output classes, depth, and hidden widths. Four pairs of tasks share the same architecture, so architecture alone does not identify the task. We train a single conditional GNN flow, supplying the task identity c c separately from the parameter graph 𝒢 {\mathcal{G}} . All architectures share the velocity network’s parameters, and none are architecture-specific. Results. sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: We proposed a permutation-equivariant GMN velocity field for learning weight distributions directly from independently trained networks, without alignment or single-trajectory construction. Experiments show our accurate generation with joint performance and similarity statistics closer to independently trained networks than with any other baseline. A single conditional model generates weights across heterogeneous architectures, transfers to unseen hidden widths, and yields individual classifiers with cross-domain performance comparable to logit ensembles. These results support incorporating weight-space permutation symmetries directly into generative architectures. Limitations and future work. Our experiments focus on fairly small networks as a first step to show accurate weight-space generation. Regardless of scalability, generation should first work at small scales without memorization. Though we believe results would hold on larger models, scaling to them is left to future work as dense graph representations cost substantial memory and compute, potentially reduced with custom GPU kernels and optimized sparse operations ( Hu et al., 2020 ) . While graph representations extend to Transformers ( Lim et al., 2024 ) , generating foundation-model weights remains an open challenge. Beyond scaling, conditioning currently uses task identifiers rather than dataset features, and we do not evaluate generation on unseen tasks. Conditioning on dataset representations, for example through Set Transformers ( Lee et al., 2019 ) or DeepSets ( Zaheer et al., 2017 ) , remains an open direction. The JWS score jointly evaluates performance and similarity, yet complementary metrics would be welcome to more broadly assess weight space generation. Nevertheless, our work opens exciting avenues to explore in weight space generation.

sections.heading: C.2 GMN Configuration
sections.text: Both GMNs use the flow-matching objective in Equation 11 , with independent standard Gaussian noise and t ∼ 𝒰 ⁡ [ 0 , 1 ] t\sim\mathcal{U}[0,1] . For these fixed-architecture experiments, we use input-layer folding on MNIST and vector-valued kernel edges on CIFAR-10, as described below. sections.heading: MNIST MLP graph representation.
sections.text: Starting from the parameter-graph construction of Lim et al. (2024) , we fold the first affine layer into node features to reduce message-passing cost (Figure 8 ). For each first-hidden-layer neuron, a shared linear encoder maps its 784 784 incoming weights and bias to a 128 128 -dimensional feature. A shared linear decoder maps its final node feature to the corresponding 785 785 parameter velocities. The remaining 1,386 1{,}386 parameters are represented by scalar-valued edges on a graph with 74 74 neuron nodes and two bias nodes. The ODE state retains all 26,506 26{,}506 parameters. Figure 8: Input-layer folding. First-layer weights and biases are encoded as first-hidden-layer node features. Hidden-unit permutations reorder these features while leaving input coordinates fixed; shared encoders and decoders therefore preserve permutation equivariance.

sections.heading: CIFAR-10 CNN graph representation.
sections.text: We build on the parameter-graph construction of Lim et al. (2024) , representing convolutional channels as nodes. Following Kofinas et al. (2024) , each edge between an input and output channel carries the nine coefficients of their 3 × 3 3\times 3 kernel in a fixed spatial order (Figure 9 ). Shared encoders map these coefficients to edge features, and shared readouts predict the corresponding nine parameter velocities. Fully connected weights and biases are represented by scalar-valued edges. Hidden-channel permutations reorder nodes and their incident edges while leaving the spatial ordering within each kernel unchanged. Figure 9: CNN kernel edge representation. One edge carries a vectorized k × k k\times k kernel.

Abstract A trained neural network can be represented by a parameter vector in high dimensions. Learning distributions over these vectors enables the generation of new models across various tasks and architectures. A central challenge is permutation symmetry: permuting hidden neurons can produce distant parameter vectors representing the same function. This introduces variations that a generative model must account for when learning from trained networks. Existing methods typically address this using networks derived from a common base model or costly approximate neuron alignment. We instead parameterize a flow-matching velocity field with a permutation-equivariant Graph Meta Network, enabling direct learning from independently trained networks without alignment. Extensive experiments show that our method closely reproduces the joint statistics of accuracy, functional similarity, and weight similarity of independently trained collections, providing evidence of generation beyond checkpoint memorization. A single conditional model also generates task-specific networks on heterogeneous architectures and generalizes to unseen hidden-width configurations. On a tabular domain-shift task, intermediate conditioning produces individual networks with performance comparable to logit ensembles across both domains. Taken together, our results show how permutation equivariance enables learning from diverse collections of independently trained networks without permutation alignment. 1 Introduction Trained network weights have emerged as a new data modality ( Unterthiner et al., 2020 ; Eilertsen et al., 2020 ; Schürholt et al., 2021 ; Navon et al., 2023 ; Navon et al., 2024 ; Lim et al., 2024 ; Putterman et al., 2024 ; Gelberg et al., 2025 ; Dayan et al., 2026 ; Knyazev et al., 2025 ; Tran et al., 2025 ; Kofinas et al., 2024 ; Kalogeropoulos et al., 2024 ) . Weight-space generative modeling promises a paradigm shift: rather than optimize neural networks, we could sample them directly from a learned distribution. Weight generation, rather than optimization, may unlock powerful capabilities, most notably conditional generation, allowing us to synthesize networks tailored to specific datasets, architectures, or domains ( Wang et al., 2026 ; Han et al., 2026 ) . Despite this potential, learning the distribution of independently trained neural networks remains a challenge. Figure 1: Hidden-unit permutations preserve the network function. Colors track each hidden unit and its incident weights. Ideally, we wish to train a generative model on large-scale network collections, spanning diverse tasks and architectures, to capture the distribution of diverse solutions. However, two functionally identical networks can have different weight matrices due to arbitrary hidden-neuron ordering (Figure 1 ). This is a practical concern as repositories like Hugging Face ( Wolf et al., 2020 ) host diverse trained networks without a common ordering or shared initialization. As such, weight-space symmetries, transformations that change weights yet preserve the function, especially permutation symmetries, are ubiquitous and thus form a fundamental obstacle in weight-space generation. To avoid this issue, prior works alter the network collections used for training. Post-hoc approaches approximately align compatible training networks to a common reference ( Ainsworth et al., 2022 ) . A priori methods instead create artificially the training collection so that alignment is not needed, typically by sampling checkpoints along the optimization trajectory of a single network ( Wang et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2025 ; Erkoç et al., 2023 ) . These strategies require either compatible architectures for alignment or control over how the training collection is constructed, restricting their applicability to existing repositories of independently trained networks. Many generators impose further limitations through fixed-dimensional parameterizations, restricting their direct reuse across architectures ( Wang et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2025 ; Erkoç et al., 2023 ; Schürholt et al., 2022 ; Schürholt et al., 2024 ; Gupta et al., 2026 ) . Moreover, sample efficiency and memorization remain challenges even within these restricted settings ( Zeng et al., 2026 ; Navon et al., 2023 ; Navon et al., 2024 ; Shamsian et al., 2024 ) . Building on this, many efforts were made toward modeling the distributions of the weights themselves. Weight-Space Generative Models. Hyper-Representations and SANE use autoencoders to learn latent representations for weight generation ( Schürholt et al., 2022 ; Schürholt et al., 2024 ) . P-diff ( Wang et al., 2024 ) combines an autoencoder with latent diffusion, a framework extended with dataset conditioning in D2NWG ( Soro et al., 2025 ) . DeepWeightFlow (DWF) operates directly in weight space, with optional PCA compression ( Gupta et al., 2026 ) , while RPG scales generation through parameter tokenization and recurrent diffusion ( Wang et al., 2025 ) . Post-Hoc Alignment. Post-hoc approaches align existing checkpoints before training the generator. SANE ( Schürholt et al., 2024 ) and DWF ( Gupta et al., 2026 ) use canonicalization methods such as Git Re-Basin ( Ainsworth et al., 2022 ) , which approximately matches weights to a common reference. Erdogan (2025) explores permutation-equivariant FM on MLP trajectory checkpoints, incorporating Git Re-Basin into the training pipeline. For Git Re-Basin, matching assumes equivalent architectures, limiting its direct applicability to heterogeneous collections. A Priori Alignment. A priori methods artificially reduce permutation variability by building dependent networks. P-diff ( Wang et al., 2024 ) collects checkpoints along an optimization trajectory, a recipe also adopted in D2NWG ( Soro et al., 2025 ) . RPG ( Wang et al., 2025 ) similarly collects fine-tuning checkpoints from pretrained models. NNiT ( Kim et al., 2026 ) builds its structurally aligned training collection using a Graph HyperNetwork with a convolutional decoder. Experiments show our accurate generation with joint performance and similarity statistics closer to independently trained networks than with any other baseline. A single conditional model generates weights across heterogeneous architectures, transfers to unseen hidden widths, and yields individual classifiers with cross-domain performance comparable to logit ensembles. These results support incorporating weight-space permutation symmetries directly into generative architectures. Limitations and future work. Our experiments focus on fairly small networks as a first step to show accurate weight-space generation. Regardless of scalability, generation should first work at small scales without memorization. Though we believe results would hold on larger models, scaling to them is left to future work as dense graph representations cost substantial memory and compute, potentially reduced with custom GPU kernels and optimized sparse operations ( Hu et al., 2020 ) . While graph representations extend to Transformers ( Lim et al., 2024 ) , generating foundation-model weights remains an open challenge. Beyond scaling, conditioning currently uses task identifiers rather than dataset features, and we do not evaluate generation on unseen tasks. Conditioning on dataset representations, for example through Set Transformers ( Lee et al., 2019 ) or DeepSets ( Zaheer et al., 2017 ) , remains an open direction. The JWS score jointly evaluates performance and similarity, yet complementary metrics would be welcome to more broadly assess weight space generation.
